source_text: Deinde uolo mihi dicatur, quoniam lego deum patrem et supra lucidam beatamque terram fundata regna eius, utrum unius et eiusdem substantiae atque naturae sint et pater et regna eius et terra. quod si ita est, iam non quasi aliam naturam, quod quasi corpus sit dei, cuneus ille gentis tenebrarum diffindit et penetrat — quod quidem ipsum esset ineffabili deformitate turpissimum — sed ipsam omnino naturam dei cuneus ille terrae tenebrarum diffindit et penetrat. rogo, cogitate ista, homines estis, rogo, cogitate ista et fugite taliumque phantasmatum sacrilegia dilaniatis, si fieri potest, pectoribus de fide uestra eradicate atque propellite. an dicturi estis non unius eiusdemque naturae illa tria esse, sed alterius patrem, alterius regna. alterius terram, ut suas naturas atque substantias habeant singula diuersas et excellentiae gradibus ordinatas ? quod si uerum est, non duas, sed quattuor naturas Manichaeus praedicare debuerat. si autem unam naturam habet pater et regna, terra uero sola diuersam, tres naturae fuerant praedicandae. aut si propterea duas dicere maluit, quia terra tenebrarum non pertinet ad deum, quaero, quomodo ad deum lucis terra pertineat. si enim et naturam habet diuersam et non eam genuit neque fecit, non ad eum pertinet et in alieno regna eius locata sunt. aut si propterea pertinet, quia uicina est, pertineat et terra tenebrarum, quae terram lucis non modo uicinitate contingit, sed etiam penetratione dissulcat. si autem genuit eam, non eam credi oportet diuersam habere naturam. quod enim genuit deus, hoc oportet credi esse, quod deus est, sicut de unigenito filio in catholica creditur. itaque ad illam fugiendam et detestandam turpitudinem uos necessitas reuocat, ut non terram quasi aliam et diuersam, sed ipsam dei naturam niger cuneus ille diffindat. quodsi non genuit, sed fecit eam deus, quaero, unde fecerit. si de se ipso, quid aliud est genuisse? si de aliena aliqua natura, quaero, utrum bona an mala. si bona, erat ergo aliqua natura bona, quae non pertinebat ad deum: quod nullo modo dicere audebitis. si autem mala, non ergo gens illa tenebrarum sola natura mala erat. an forte iam inde adsumpserat partem aliquam deus, quam in terram lucis conuerteret et super illam sua regna stabiliret? de tota ergo id fecisset, ut iam olim mala natura nulla esset. quodsi non de aliena substantia fecit terram lucis. restat, ut eam de nihilo fecerit.
thought_title: Mani's threefold land of light collapses into one nature, which the wedge of darkness penetrates
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing the implications of Mani's own words about God the Father and his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land.
pass_a_gloss: Next I want it to be said to me, since I read God the Father and his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land, whether the Father and his kingdoms and the land are of one and the same substance and nature. But if this is so, now not as if another nature, as if it were a body of God, does that wedge of the race of darkness split and penetrate — which very thing indeed would be most foul with unspeakable deformity — but that wedge of the land of darkness splits and penetrates the very nature of God entirely. I ask, think about these things, you are human beings, I ask, think about these things and flee, and tear out and drive away from your faith, if it can be done, the sacrileges of such fantasies from your lacerated hearts. Or are you going to say that those three things are not of one and the same nature, but the Father is of one, the kingdoms of another, the land of another, so that each single one has its own natures and substances, diverse and ordered by degrees of excellence? But if this is true, Mani ought to have proclaimed not two, but four natures. But if the Father and the kingdoms have one nature, but the land alone has a diverse one, three natures ought to have been proclaimed. Or if he preferred to say two for this reason, because the land of darkness does not belong to God, I ask how the land of light belongs to God. For if it both has a diverse nature and he did not beget it nor make it, it does not belong to him and his kingdoms are located in another's property. Or if it belongs for this reason, because it is neighboring, let the land of darkness also belong, which not only touches the land of light by nearness, but also furrows it by penetration. But if he begot it, it ought not to be believed to have a diverse nature. For what God has begotten, this ought to be believed to be what God is, just as is believed in the Catholic Church about the only-begotten Son. And so necessity calls you back to that foulness to be fled and detested, so that not the land as if another and diverse, but the very nature of God does that black wedge split. But if God did not beget it, but made it, I ask from what he made it. If from himself, what else is it than to have begotten? If from some other nature, I ask whether it was good or evil. If good, therefore there was some good nature which did not belong to God: which you will in no way dare to say. But if evil, therefore that race of darkness was not the only evil nature. Or perhaps God had already taken from there some part, which he might turn into the land of light and upon it establish his kingdoms? Therefore he would have done it from the whole, so that already long ago there would be no evil nature. But if he did not make the land of light from another's substance, it remains that he made it from nothing.

choices.english: that wedge of the race of darkness
choices.why: Keeps the military/geometric image of a wedge as in the previous section, and 'race' for gens matches the earlier rendering of the dark people.
rejected: the wedge of the nation of darkness

choices.why: Preserves the violent physical force of the verbs, which Augustine uses to expose the bodily conception of God.
Keeps the strong image of tearing, matching Augustine's rhetorical urgency; 'hearts' for pectoribus fits the moral-spiritual sense.
Matches the phrase used in the following section ('excellentiae gradibus ordinatas') and keeps the technical sense of ranked natures.
rejected: set in order by steps of excellence

choices.term: in alieno regna eius locata sunt
choices.english: his kingdoms are located in another's property
choices.why: 'Alieno' as 'another's property' brings out the legal/ownership sense Augustine is pressing: if the land is not God's, his kingdoms sit on someone else's ground.
rejected: his kingdoms are placed in a foreign thing
his kingdoms are situated in what belongs to another

choices.why: 'Furrows' keeps the agricultural image of cutting into the land, which suits the land of light being treated as soil.

pass_b_english: Next, since I read of God the Father, and of his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land, I want someone to tell me whether the Father, his kingdoms, and the land are of one and the same substance and nature. If that is so, then that wedge of the race of darkness no longer splits and penetrates what is, as it were, another nature that is the body of God—which itself would be foul with unspeakable deformity—but that wedge of the land of darkness splits and penetrates the very nature of God itself. Think about this, I beg you—you are human beings—think about this and flee; and with torn hearts, if it can be done, root these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your faith and drive them away. Or will you say that those three are not of one and the same nature, but that the Father has one nature, the kingdoms another, and the land another, so that each has its own distinct natures and substances, ordered by degrees of excellence? If that is true, Mani should have proclaimed not two natures but four. But if the Father and the kingdoms have one nature, and the land alone has a different one, then three natures should have been proclaimed. Or if he preferred to say two because the land of darkness does not belong to God, I ask how the land of light does belong to God. For if it has a different nature and he neither begot it nor made it, it does not belong to him, and his kingdoms are located in another's property. Or if it belongs to him because it is nearby, then the land of darkness also belongs to him, since it not only touches the land of light by nearness but even furrows it by penetration. But if he begot it, then we ought not to believe that it has a different nature. For what God has begotten, we ought to believe is what God is, as the Catholic Church believes concerning the only-begotten Son. And so necessity drives you back to that foulness to be fled and detested: that the black wedge splits not the land as something other and different, but the very nature of God. But if God did not beget the land but made it, I ask from what he made it. If from himself, what else is that but begetting? If from some other nature, I ask whether it was good or evil. If good, then there was some good nature that did not belong to God—which you will never dare to say. If evil, then that race of darkness was not the only evil nature. Or perhaps God had already taken some part from it, which he turned into the land of light and upon which he established his kingdoms? Then he should have done this with the whole of it, so that no evil nature would remain. But if he did not make the land of light from another substance, it remains that he made it from nothing.

problems.source_quote: ad illam fugiendam et detestandam turpitudinem
problems.why: 'Turpitudinem' = 'foulness/shamefulness'; 'conclusion' is added, not in Latin. Augustine says 'to that foulness to be fled and detested'.
problems.fix: to that foulness to be fled and detested
problems.ruling: 'turpitudinem' = 'foulness/shamefulness'; 'conclusion' is added, not in Latin; changes the noun's meaning.

edits.new: that foulness to be fled and detested

fixed: Changed 'that foul and detestable conclusion' to 'that foulness to be fled and detested' because the source 'ad illam fugiendam et detestandam turpitudinem' means 'to that foulness to be fled and detested'; 'conclusion' is not in the Latin.

problems.why: The Latin 'fugite' has two objects understood: first 'ista' (these things), then 'sacrilegia' (the sacrileges). The English 'flee it' is vague; 'flee these things and the sacrileges of such fantasies' is needed.

edits.old: Think about this, I beg you—you are human beings—think about this and flee it.
edits.new: Think about this, I beg you—you are human beings—think about this and flee these things.

fixed: Changed 'flee it' to 'flee these things' because the Latin 'fugite' has 'ista' (these things) as its object, not a singular 'it'; the sacrileges are the second object of the following clause.

problems.why: English omits 'talium phantasmatum' (of such fantasies), losing the specific object of fleeing before the next clause.
problems.fix: flee from such fantasies and these things
problems.ruling: 'fugite taliumque phantasmatum sacrilegia'—English 'flee these things' omits 'sacrilegia' and 'talium phantasmatum' entirely.

problems.why: Dilaniatis means 'torn/riven,' but 'lacerated' suggests wounded; more importantly, the syntax is wrong—the hearts are not already lacerated but are to be torn (root out from).
problems.fix: tear these sacrileges of such fantasies from your torn hearts
problems.ruling: 'dilaniatis...pectoribus' are ablative to be torn apart, not pre-existing 'lacerated hearts'; syntax and agency are wrong.

edits.old: think about this and flee these things.
edits.new: think about this and flee from such fantasies.

edits.old: Tear these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your lacerated hearts, if it can be done, and drive them from your faith.
edits.new: Tear these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your torn hearts, if it can be done, and drive them from your faith.

fixed: Added 'from such fantasies' to restore the omitted object of fleeing (source: 'fugite taliumque phantasmatum sacrilegia').
Changed 'lacerated' to 'torn' to reflect 'dilaniatis' as the state of the hearts from which the sacrileges are to be rooted out.

problems.quote: God the Father and his kingdoms are founded upon the bright and blessed land
problems.source_quote: lego deum patrem et supra lucidam beatamque terram fundata regna eius
problems.why: fundata agrees only with regna: he reads of the Father, and of kingdoms founded on the land. The Father is not founded there.
problems.fix: since I read of God the Father, and of his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land
problems.ruling: "fundata regna eius" – only the kingdoms are founded on the land; English makes the Father also founded upon it, misstating the doctrine.

problems.quote: flee from such fantasies. Tear these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your torn hearts, if it can be done, and drive them from your faith
problems.source_quote: fugite taliumque phantasmatum sacrilegia dilaniatis, si fieri potest, pectoribus de fide uestra eradicate atque propellite
problems.why: Flee stands alone. Torn hearts are the manner; the sacrileges are rooted out of faith, not torn out of the heart.
problems.fix: flee; and, with your hearts torn, if it can be done, root these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your faith and drive them off
problems.ruling: "dilaniatis pectoribus" is an ablative absolute with eradicate: 'with torn breasts, root out of your faith'; English wrongly says sacrileges torn out of hearts, shifting 'de fide uestra'.

edits.old: since I read that God the Father and his kingdoms are founded upon the bright and blessed land
edits.new: since I read of God the Father, and of his kingdoms founded upon the bright and blessed land

edits.old: think about this and flee from such fantasies. Tear these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your torn hearts, if it can be done, and drive them from your faith
edits.new: think about this and flee; and with torn hearts, if it can be done, root these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your faith and drive them away

fixed: mistranslation fundata: fixed — fundata agrees only with regna in 'supra lucidam beatamque terram fundata regna eius', so Father is not founded there.
mistranslation fugite/eradicate: fixed — 'fugite' stands alone and 'dilaniatis pectoribus' is manner while rooting is 'de fide uestra eradicate atque propellite'.
earlier edit to 'that foulness to be fled and detested': no edit — correctly renders 'fugiendam et detestandam turpitudinem'.
earlier edit 'flee it' to 'flee these': superseded by the fugite fix above; no separate edit.
earlier edit to 'flee from such fantasies': fixed as part of the fugite fix above, since 'fugite' takes no object.
earlier edit 'lacerated' to 'torn hearts': superseded by the fugite fix above, since 'dilaniatis pectoribus' is manner for 'de fide uestra eradicate'.

dismissed.quote: Tear these sacrileges of such fantasies out of your torn hearts
dismissed.why: Misreads 'dilaniatis...pectoribus' as 'torn hearts' rather than 'with torn/beset hearts'; 'dilaniatis' is dative/ablative plural, modifying 'pectoribus', not 'sacrilegia'.
dismissed.note: 'Out of your torn hearts, if it can be done' is a fair loose rendering of the ablative absolute 'dilaniatis pectoribus'; the meaning is kept.

last_rejected.quote: what is, as it were, another nature that is the body of God—which itself would be foul with unspeakable deformity
last_rejected.source_quote: quasi aliam naturam, quod quasi corpus sit dei, cuneus ille gentis tenebrarum diffindit et penetrat — quod quidem ipsum esset ineffabili deformitate turpissimum
last_rejected.why: The foulness judges the splitting itself; the body is only “as it were” God’s body, not what is foul.
last_rejected.fix: does not split and penetrate what is, as it were, another nature—since it is, as it were, God’s body—which act would itself be foul with unspeakable deformity
last_rejected.ruling: The English's relative clause 'which itself would be foul' is ambiguous but 'quod quidem ipsum' refers to the whole splitting; a reader can take it so. Not a meaning change.
